raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade with sacubitril, a prodrug whose active metabolite inhibits neprilysin. The mechanistic rationale is simultaneous suppression of maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone signaling and augmentation of natriuretic peptide, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathways, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, antifibrotic signaling, and reverse remodeling [1]. This strategy was developed after isolated neprilysin inhibition and vasopeptidase inhibition proved insufficient or limited by angioedema; selective ARNI preserves renin–angiotensin blockade without concomitant ACE inhibition.

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is PARADIGM-HF, which randomized 8399 ambulatory symptomatic patients to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril and showed significant reductions in cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalization, and all-cause mortality [2]. Subsequent analyses strengthened biological plausibility and clinical relevance: sacubitril/valsartan slowed clinical progression among survivors [3], reduced both sudden death and pump-failure death [4], retained benefit across baseline systolic blood pressure strata despite more hypotension [5], and slowed estimated glomerular filtration rate decline compared with enalapril despite modestly increasing albuminuria [6]. Reduced loop-diuretic requirement in PARADIGM-HF further suggests improved congestion biology or hemodynamics [7].

Evidence for early initiation has expanded the drug from a stable outpatient therapy to a hospitalization-to-discharge strategy. In PIONEER-HF, hemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF had greater NT-proBNP reduction with sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, or angioedema [8]. Exploratory PIONEER-HF analyses suggested fewer early serious clinical events [9], and biomarker studies showed early reductions in troponin and soluble ST2 with increased urinary cGMP, consistent with reduced myocardial injury and wall stress [10]. Benefit and tolerability appeared broadly consistent across achieved dose levels [11]. TRANSITION and TITRATION provide pragmatic initiation data: gradual uptitration is often useful in lower blood pressure or renin–angiotensin system inhibitor–naïve patients, but pre-discharge and early post-discharge initiation are both feasible after stabilization [12–14].

Reverse remodeling is an important mechanistic bridge. In PROVE-HF, reductions in NT-proBNP after sacubitril/valsartan initiation correlated with improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction [15]. EVALUATE-HF did not significantly reduce aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril but did show favorable remodeling and health-status signals [16]. These findings support the concept that ARNI benefit is not merely diuretic or vasodilatory, but linked to sustained structural and neurohormonal change.

In heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, efficacy is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT first showed greater NT-proBNP reduction than valsartan in HFpEF [17]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested greater benefit in women and in patients with ejection fraction below the higher “preserved” range [18,19]. A pooled PARADIGM-HF/PARAGON-HF analysis demonstrated a continuous attenuation of benefit as ejection fraction rises, with the clearest effect below normal ejection fraction [20]. PARALLAX reduced NT-proBNP but did not improve 6-minute walk distance versus individualized background therapy [21]. PARAGLIDE-HF, enrolling patients with EF >40% after worsening heart failure, showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and signals favoring patients with EF ≤60%, at the cost of more symptomatic hypotension [22]. Participant-level pooling of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF supports reduction in worsening heart-failure events and renal events, particularly when EF is below normal [23].

Important limitations remain. Trial run-in phases selected for tolerability in PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF, so real-world hypotension, renal dysfunction, and cost barriers require active management. Sacubitril/valsartan should not be combined with ACE inhibitors, requires a washout after ACE inhibitors, and is avoided in patients with prior angioedema. Advanced HFrEF is less certain: LIFE was designed for very high-risk patients [24], and its randomized results did not show superiority over valsartan for NT-proBNP or clinical outcomes, with more non–life-threatening hyperkalemia [25]. After acute myocardial infarction, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or incident heart failure versus ramipril [26], so routine post-infarction replacement of ACE inhibition is not established.

Current guidelines place sacubitril/valsartan among foundational HFrEF therapies, preferably replacing ACE inhibitor or ARB in symptomatic patients and often started de novo when clinically appropriate [27,28]. Contemporary focused updates also recognize a role across mildly reduced ejection fraction, while HFpEF recommendations are weaker and most compelling near the lower EF range [29,30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan is a disease-modifying therapy with robust HFrEF outcome benefit, practical evidence for early initiation, plausible remodeling mechanisms, and selective—but not universal—benefit beyond classic HFrEF.
